import itertools
from pysat.solvers import Glucose3

n = 23
solver = Glucose3()

# Variables for edges
def var(i, j):
    if i > j:
        i, j = j, i
    return i * n + j + 1

# Degree constraints
# We can use cardinality constraints, but since degree is small, we can just use combinations
# Actually, PySAT has CardEnc
from pysat.card import CardEnc

for i in range(n):
    edges = [var(i, j) for j in range(n) if i != j]
    # degree >= 3
    cnf1 = CardEnc.atleast(lits=edges, bound=3, vpool=None)
    for clause in cnf1.clauses:
        solver.add_clause(clause)
    # degree <= 6
    cnf2 = CardEnc.atmost(lits=edges, bound=6, vpool=None)
    for clause in cnf2.clauses:
        solver.add_clause(clause)

# No 3-cycles
for i, j, k in itertools.combinations(range(n), 3):
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, j), -var(j, k), -var(i, k)])

# No 4-cycles
for i, j, k, l in itertools.combinations(range(n), 4):
    # 3 possible 4-cycles for 4 vertices
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, j), -var(j, k), -var(k, l), -var(l, i)])
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, j), -var(j, l), -var(l, k), -var(k, i)])
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, k), -var(k, j), -var(j, l), -var(l, i)])

# No 5-cycles
for c in itertools.combinations(range(n), 5):
    # 12 possible 5-cycles for 5 vertices
    for p in itertools.permutations(c[1:]):
        # cycle is c[0], p[0], p[1], p[2], p[3]
        # to avoid duplicates, we can enforce p[0] < p[3]
        if p[0] < p[3]:
            solver.add_clause([-var(c[0], p[0]), -var(p[0], p[1]), -var(p[1], p[2]), -var(p[2], p[3]), -var(p[3], c[0])])

print("Solving...")
if solver.solve():
    print("SAT")
    model = solver.get_model()
    edges = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if model[var(i, j) - 1] > 0:
                edges.append((i, j))
    print(edges)
else:
    print("UNSAT")
